content: The Enterobacteriaceae family is a large group of bacteria that includes many well-known pathogens, such as Salmonella and Escherichia coli. Genetic analyses classify them within the Proteobacteria phylum, and they are assigned their own order, Enterobacteriales. However, in some cases, this order may also encompass certain related environmental samples. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family are rod-shaped bacteria, typically measuring between 1 and 5 micrometers in length. Like other Proteobacteria, they are Gram-negative, meaning they do not retain the crystal violet stain used in Gram staining. These bacteria are facultative anaerobes, which means they can survive in both oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor environments. They ferment sugars to produce lactic acid and other metabolic byproducts. Additionally, they have the ability to reduce nitrate to nitrite. Unlike many other similar bacteria, most Enterobacteriaceae lack cytochrome C oxidase, although there are exceptions, such as Plesiomonas. Many members of this family are motile, possessing multiple flagella that allow them to move. However, some genera within the family are non-motile. They do not form spores, and most are catalase-positive, meaning they produce the enzyme catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide. An exception to this is certain strains of Shigella dysenteriae, which are catalase-negative. A significant number of Enterobacteriaceae species are part of the normal gut flora in the intestines of humans and other animals. Others are found in environmental settings such as water and soil, or they act as parasites on various animals and plants. Among these bacteria, Escherichia coli (E. coli) is particularly notable as a model organism. Its genetics and biochemistry have been extensively studied, making it one of the most important organisms in scientific research. Most members of the Enterobacteriaceae family possess peritrichous Type I fimbriae, which are hair-like structures that play a crucial role in the adhesion of bacterial cells to their host tissues. The genera within the Enterobacteriaceae family include the following: Alishewanella Alterococcus Aquamonas Aranicola Arsenophonus Azotivirga Blochmannia Brenneria Buchnera Budvicia Buttiauxella Cedecea Citrobacter Dickeya Edwardsiella Enterobacter Erwinia (e.g., Erwinia amylovora) Escherichia (e.g., Escherichia coli) Ewingella Grimontella Hafnia Klebsiella (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae) Kluyvera Leclercia Leminorella Moellerella Morganella Obesumbacterium Pantoea Pectobacterium Candidatus Phlomobacter Photorhabdus (e.g., Photorhabdus luminescens) Plesiomonas (e.g., Plesiomonas shigelloides) Pragia Proteus (e.g., Proteus vulgaris) Providencia Rahnella Raoultella Salmonella Samsonia Serratia (e.g., Serratia marcescens) Shigella Sodalis Tatumella Trabulsiella Wigglesworthia Xenorhabdus Yersinia (e.g., Yersinia pestis) Yokenella
